finding.claim: /transfer never checks that amount is positive. A negative amount passes the balance check and reverses the transfer, so the attacker takes money from any other account. Unlike /withdraw, which checks amount <= 0, there is no guard.
finding.source: Authenticated user's JSON body: 'to' (any victim account name) and 'amount' (negative number)
finding.sink: BAL[g.user] -= amount and BAL[to] += amount (lines 13-14), which move funds in the wrong direction

trace.note: amount = request.json['amount'] is attacker-controlled and has no type or sign validation
BAL[g.user] < amount is false for a negative amount, so the check passes
BAL[g.user] -= (-X) increases the attacker's balance by X
BAL[to] += (-X) decreases the victim's balance by X, with no check that the victim stays non-negative

finding.guards_checked: Only the BAL[g.user] < amount check exists, and it does not catch negative values. There is no sign check, no type check (a string or float would also be accepted or raise a 500), and no check that the recipient consents. The /withdraw route has the amount <= 0 guard, which shows the check was intended.

verdict.guard_found: none (only BAL[g.user] < amount at bank.py:11, which a negative amount passes; the amount <= 0 guard exists only in /withdraw at line 21)
verdict.reason: bank.py:9-14 take an unvalidated attacker-supplied amount, so a negative value passes the check at line 11 and then adds to the sender's balance (line 13) and subtracts from the victim's (line 14), with no sign check as /withdraw has at line 21.

finding.claim: No authentication is set up. g.user is read in both routes, but the file has no before_request hook, session handling or token check that sets it. If a hook outside this file does not set it, the endpoints fail on every call. If something else sets g.user from an untrusted value, the endpoints inherit that weakness. In this file the identity is unverified.
finding.sink: BAL[g.user] reads and writes in /transfer and /withdraw

trace.note: The app is created with no auth middleware, before_request hook, or login route
g.user is used as the identity with no assignment anywhere in the file

finding.guards_checked: Searched the only file in the directory (bank.py) for any g.user assignment, before_request, or decorator-based auth and found none. This is lower confidence, because auth may live in another module that is not present in this directory.

verdict.reason: bank.py:11 and :21 read g.user, which is never assigned in the only file present (bank.py:3 has no hook). Flask would raise AttributeError and return a 500, so no bypass is shown. Whether it is exploitable depends on external code that sets g.user, and none is available here.

finding.claim: /transfer debits the sender before it looks up the recipient. If 'to' is not an existing account, BAL[to] raises KeyError and returns a 500 after the sender has already lost the funds. Concurrent requests also race: the check-then-act on the shared BAL dict is not atomic, so two parallel transfers or withdrawals can overspend.
finding.source: Authenticated user's JSON body: a nonexistent 'to' value, or concurrent parallel requests
finding.sink: BAL[g.user] -= amount (line 13), executed before BAL[to] += amount (line 14)

trace.note: The balance check and the later update are not atomic, so concurrent requests can both pass the check (TOCTOU)
KeyError on an unknown 'to' aborts the request after the debit, with no rollback

finding.guards_checked: No lock, transaction or recipient existence check. Under a threaded server, the check-then-act race exists. Race exploitability depends on the deployment.

verdict.reason: bank.py:13 debits BAL[g.user] before bank.py:14 `BAL[to] += amount` raises KeyError for an unknown recipient, with no recipient check, lock or rollback, and the balance check at bank.py:11 is a non-atomic check-then-act.
